problemStatement:
Problem Statement:
 Continuous heart-rate and breathing monitoring is central to patient safety, yet it depends on contact sensors such as ECG electrodes, chest straps and finger clips. These become impractical precisely where monitoring matters most: adhesives irritate the fragile skin of neonates and burn patients, shared probes carry cross-infection risk in isolation wards, trailing wires restrict drivers and elderly patients, and motion or moisture degrade the signal. Sensors that must be worn and kept in place are often removed or mispositioned, forcing clinicians to trade comfort and hygiene against continuity of data and leaving a monitoring gap for the patients who most need continuous observation. 
Proposed Solution: 
EchoVitals is a contactless vital-sign monitor that measures heart rate and breathing rate with no electrodes, straps or wires. A 60 GHz frequency-modulated continuous-wave (FMCW) radar module, mounted 0.4–1.5 m from the subject, tracks the phase of the chest-wall reflection to recover sub-millimetre cardiac motion beneath the much larger movement of breathing. Its onboard DSP performs ranging and signal extraction and streams rate values to an ESP32 microcontroller, which forwards them to a host layer that validates, smooths and displays live heart and breathing rate on a dashboard and optional OLED. The radar senses through clothing and bedding and uses no camera, so it is comfortable, hygienic and privacy-preserving, and the whole platform runs from a single 5 V supply.
Innovation and Novelty:
Our contribution is not the radar itself but a validated, application-level system built around it. First, a validity-gating layer uses the module’s reported target count and range to reject readings when no subject is present or the subject leaves the sensing zone, preventing stale or spurious vitals. Second, we evaluate rigorously rather than anecdotally: heart rate against a reference pulse oximeter and breathing rate against a timed manual count, across multiple volunteers and through fabric barriers, reporting measured error instead of datasheet claims. Third, the design is low-cost and reproducible, using one radar module, one microcontroller and open-source Python. Together these turn a sensing component into a trustworthy monitoring platform for infants, infectious-disease wards, drivers and bedside care, demonstrated live on working hardware.

workingPrinciple: EchoVitals measures heart rate and breathing rate from chest-wall motion using a 60 GHz frequency-modulated continuous-wave (FMCW) radar module, with no skin contact. Workflow: (1) The radar transmits low-power frequency chirps toward the subject’s chest from 0.4–1.5 m. (2) Each echo is mixed with the transmitted chirp to produce a beat signal whose frequency encodes distance; a range-FFT isolates the chest wall as a single range bin. (3) The phase of that bin is tracked across successive chirps. Because phase shifts in proportion to displacement, it recovers breathing motion (millimetre scale, about 0.1–0.3 Hz) and the much smaller cardiac motion (about 0.2–0.5 mm, 1–2 Hz). (4) The module’s onboard DSP separates these frequency bands and outputs breathing rate, heart rate, target range and target count over a serial (UART) link. (5) An ESP32 microcontroller reads each frame and forwards it to a Python host layer. (6) The host layer applies validity gating, discarding readings when no subject is present or the subject leaves the monitoring zone, then smooths the remaining values with a short moving average. (7) Live heart rate and breathing rate appear on a dashboard and an optional OLED display. Accuracy is validated against a reference pulse oximeter and a timed manual breath count

potentialImpact:
Who benefits: neonates and burn patients, whose skin cannot tolerate adhesive electrodes; patients in isolation and infectious-disease wards, where every shared probe is a cross-infection risk; elderly people living alone or in care homes, who can be monitored in bed or in the bathroom without wearing anything; drivers, pilots and train operators, whose alertness and heart health affect many other lives; and ordinary households that want sleep and wellness insight without straps or cameras.

How it improves current standards: vital signs are often spot-checked a few times a day because continuous monitoring needs wires, adhesives and patient cooperation. EchoVitals makes continuous monitoring effortless: nothing is attached, nothing needs cleaning between patients, and nothing can be forgotten, loosened or removed. It protects privacy because it captures no images, making monitoring acceptable in bedrooms and bathrooms where cameras never could be. Built from low-cost, off-the-shelf parts and open-source software, it can be replicated at a much lower cost than conventional bedside monitors, bringing continuous monitoring within reach of small clinics, care homes and families.

Looking ahead, the same platform can raise alerts for breathing pauses or abnormal heart rate, track sleep quality, and extend to multi-bed wards. EchoVitals is a research prototype, not a certified medical device, and our testing against reference instruments is designed to show honestly where it can be trusted.
auraDemoHighlight:
Imagine a heartbeat measured from across the room. EchoVitals reads a person’s heart rate and breathing rate without touching them: no electrodes, no straps, no clips and no camera. Judges can sit in front of it and watch their own vital signs appear live on screen, beside a standard pulse oximeter, so the comparison happens in real time rather than on a slide.

What makes it stand out:

Genuinely contactless: it works through clothing, and we will show it working with fabric placed in between.

Private and hygienic: no images are captured and nothing touches the patient, which suits infants, burn and isolation patients, and elderly care.

Affordable and reproducible: a handful of low-cost components and open-source code that any college lab can rebuild.

Honest by design: when the person leaves or the signal is poor, the display flags the reading as unreliable instead of showing a confident but wrong number.
safetyPrecautions:
- Low-voltage: powered only by a 5 V USB power bank, no mains connection.
- Low-power radar sensor on a stable stand; nothing touches the body.
- Enclosed, insulated wiring with no exposed conductors.
- No moving parts, heat or chemicals.
- Research prototype, not a medical device; volunteers consent and a team member is always present.

abstract.extractedText:
EchoVitals

A radar-based platform for contactless vital health sign sensing.

 Heart rate and breathing monitoring in settings where wearable contact-based sensors are impractical.

Arman Israfil1,  Sk Sahil Ahamed1,  Md Qais Khan1,  Md Faizan1

1 Dept. of Electronics and Communication Engineering

Aliah University

Kolkata, India

Abstract: EchoVitals is a low-cost, contactless platform that measures heart rate and breathing rate by reflecting a 60 GHz frequency-modulated continuous-wave (FMCW) radar signal off the chest wall, with no electrodes, straps, or wires. Contact-based sensors are impractical for burn and infectious patients, infants, and high-stress operators, and are uncomfortable for long-term wear (Fig. 1). An integrated FMCW radar module performs on-chip range-gating and phase extraction to separate the heartbeat's sub-millimetre motion from the much larger motion of breathing, and a lightweight host-side layer validates and smooths the resulting readings. We target accuracy comparable to the module's rated performance across the deployment settings in Fig. 2.

Index Terms : contactless vital-sign monitoring, 60 GHz FMCW radar, mmWave sensing, heart rate, respiration rate.

I. Introduction

A. Problem statement & why and where contact-based devices fail :Continuous contact sensing such as ECG pads, chest straps, and clip-on pulse oximeters  requires wiring. Also, for adhesive types, skin contact is impractical in case of burn and infectious patients, easily irritated for neonates(infants), and restrictive for drivers and pilots. Fig. 1 summarises the recurring failure modes this creates.

Fig. 1. Recurring failure modes of contact-based vital sign sensors.

B. Proposed solution:  EchoVitals senses the chest wall directly using a compact radar-on-module: a self-contained transceiver and antenna array paired with an onboard digital signal processor that runs the full frequency-modulated continuous-wave (FMCW) ranging and vital-sign extraction pipeline in hardware. The short wavelength at this frequency band gives the module's phase-based ranging technique the sensitivity needed to resolve the chest wall's sub-millimetre cardiac displacement beneath its much larger respiratory motion, with no external amplification stage. The module reports breathing rate, heart rate, target range, and target count over a standard serial link; the ESP32 microcontroller forwards these values to a host script for validation, smoothing, and display.

C. Deployment settings:  This applies wherever continuous contact sensing is impractical: infants and NICU care, burn and infectious-disease wards, drivers, pilots and train operators, elderly bed and bathroom monitoring, smart mattresses for sleep tracking, and fitness or gym use i.e mapped in Fig. 2. Longer-range scenarios such as search-and-rescue remain future work: the module's rated sensing range (0.4–1.5 m) is built for a fixed, near-body mount, not a moving drone.

Fig. 2. Target deployment settings for contactless vital sign sensing.

II. Proposed Implementation

We build around a single integrated 60 GHz FMCW radar-on-module, which keeps the sensing hardware to one component and removes the need for a discrete amplification stage. The module communicates over a 4-wire serial link (5V, GND, TX, RX) directly to the ESP32 microcontroller; Table I lists the resulting stack.

III. Methodology

The sensing stage is built around a single-chip 60 GHz FMCW radar transceiver. The module emits a sequence of linear frequency chirps and mixes each received echo with the transmitted chirp to produce an intermediate frequency beat signal whose frequency encodes target range. A range-FFT across each chirp resolves the subject's chest wall as a single range bin, and the phase of that bin is tracked chirp-to-chirp to recover sub-millimetre surface displacement,  the basis of micro-Doppler vital-sign sensing. Onboard firmware separates this phase history into two frequency bands: a low-frequency, high-amplitude component corresponding to respiration, and a higher-frequency, low-amplitude component corresponding to the heartbeat, and reports both as periodic rate values together with a target count and range estimate.

On the host side, EchoVitals treats these periodic values as a lightweight telemetry stream rather than a raw waveform. A parsing layer reads each frame; a validity gate cross-checks the reported target count and range against the expected monitoring zone and discards frames where no subject is present or the subject has left the sensing envelope; and a short moving-average stage smooths the surviving readings before they reach the display. The signal-processing burden , chirp generation, range-gating, and respiration/cardiac band separation is carried entirely by the radar module's onboard DSP, keeping the host implementation small and auditable. The complete signal path and power distribution are shown in Fig. 3.

Fig. 3. 60 GHz FMCW system block diagram showing signal path and power distribution.

IV. Desired Output and Expected Results

A working prototype displaying live heart rate and breathing rate on a bedside dashboard, mounted 0.4–1.5 m from a seated or lying subject. We will validate against a reference pulse oximeter for heart rate and a manual 60-second breath count for breathing rate, across at least four consenting team volunteers, and record the module's own reported target confidence alongside each reading. Manufacturer-published figures for this class of module report respiratory accuracy around 90% and cardiac accuracy in the 85–95% range depending on test conditions; we report our own measured error rather than assuming a datasheet figure holds in our setup.

V. Conclusion

EchoVitals shows that reliable, contact-free vital-sign monitoring is achievable with a single integrated 60 GHz FMCW radar module, a microcontroller, and a lightweight validation layer  without the fragile analog front end or complex filtering pipeline that raw-radar approaches typically require. The system measures heart rate and breathing directly from chest-wall motion, targets accuracy comparable to its sensor class through reference-validated testing and is designed for deployment across the patient groups and environments outlined in this proposal. It offers a practical, low-cost foundation for non-contact patient monitoring that can be extended toward broader clinical and field use.
